entries.text: When you deposit $1,000 into a bank, you might think it just sits in a vault, waiting for you.
But banks are only required to keep a small fraction—say 10%—as a reserve. The rest is fair game for lending.
The bank lends that $900 to someone else. This new loan becomes a deposit in another bank.
This process repeats. That $900 generates another $810 loan, then $729, and so on. This is the money multiplier effect.
Fractional reserve lending fuels economic growth by expanding credit, but it requires trust and stability to function.
